goals: Put the verb in second position, also after a time or a place
Ask W-questions and yes/no questions and answer with ja, nein or doch
Build the sentence bracket with modal verbs and separable verbs
Give instructions with the imperative for du, ihr and Sie
Say when things happen with um, am, im, von … bis and ab

grammar.explain:
In a German statement, the conjugated verb (the verb with the personal ending) is always in **position 2**. This is one of the most important rules of German word order.
Position 2 means the second *part* of the sentence, not always the second word. Position 1 is often the subject (**Ich** trinke am Morgen Kaffee.), but it can also be a time or a place. A group like **am Morgen**, **um acht Uhr** or **in Berlin** counts as one part.
When something other than the subject comes first, the verb stays in position 2 and the subject moves right behind it. This is called **inversion**: **Ich arbeite heute.** → **Heute arbeite ich.** The meaning stays the same; the time or place just gets more attention. Words like **heute**, **dann**, **am Abend**, **um sieben Uhr** and **im Sommer** often start a sentence.
The little words **und**, **aber** and **oder** do not count. They stand before position 1, so the order after them does not change: **Ali kocht und Sara liest.**
Careful: English says *Today I work*, but German never allows **Heute ich arbeite**. Persian puts the verb at the end, but in a German statement it must come second: **Ich wohne in Teheran**, not **Ich in Teheran wohne**.

title.t: Wo wohnst du? Wohnst du hier?

grammar.explain:
German has two main kinds of questions. **W-questions** ask for information and start with a question word: **wer** *who*, **was** *what*, **wo** *where*, **woher** *where from*, **wann** *when*, **wie** *how*, **wie viel** *how much*, **wie alt** *how old*. The question word is in position 1, the verb in position 2, and then usually the subject: **Wo wohnst du?** **Wann kommt der Bus?** With **wer** the question word is itself the subject: **Wer kocht heute?**
**Yes/no questions** have no question word. The verb moves to **position 1**, and the subject comes right after it: **Du wohnst in Berlin.** → **Wohnst du in Berlin?** The rest of the sentence stays where it was, and your voice goes up at the end.
The answer to a yes/no question is **ja** or **nein**. But if the question is negative (with **nicht** or **kein**) and you want to say *yes*, use **doch**: **Hast du keinen Hunger?** – **Doch, ich habe Hunger.** If you agree with the negative question, say **nein**: **Kommst du nicht mit?** – **Nein, ich habe keine Zeit.**
Careful: German has no helper verb like English *do*. *Do you live here?* is simply **Wohnst du hier?** Persian often keeps the statement order and only changes the intonation, but in German the verb must move to the front. Also, **wer** looks like English *where*, but it means *who*; *where* is **wo**. And to ask for a name, say **Wie heißt du?**, not **Was heißt du?**

grammar.explain:
Many German sentences have a verb in two parts. The conjugated part stays in **position 2**, and the second part goes to the very **end** of the sentence. Everything else stands between them, as if inside a **sentence bracket**.
There are two kinds. With a **modal verb** (**können**, **müssen**, **wollen**, **möchten**), the modal verb is in position 2 and the other verb goes to the end as an **infinitive**: **Ich muss heute arbeiten.** **Maryam kann sehr gut kochen.** With a **separable verb**, the main part is in position 2 and the prefix goes to the end: **Ich rufe meine Oma an.** **Wir kaufen im Supermarkt ein.**
Inversion does not change the bracket: **Heute muss ich arbeiten.** **Am Abend sieht Amir fern.** In a yes/no question the conjugated part is in position 1, and the end stays at the end: **Kannst du heute mitkommen?** If a separable verb comes with a modal verb, it is the infinitive, so it stays together at the end: **Ich muss um sechs Uhr aufstehen.** The word **nicht** usually comes just before the end: **Ich muss heute nicht arbeiten.**
Careful: English keeps the verbs together (*I must work today*), so learners often say **Ich muss arbeiten heute**. That is wrong; the infinitive goes to the end. Don't give the infinitive an ending (**Ich kann schwimmen**, not **Ich kann schwimme**), and don't forget the prefix: **Ich stehe um sieben Uhr** is not complete without **auf**.

grammar.explain:
The imperative is the form for instructions, requests and advice: *Come!* *Please call me!* German has three forms, because there are three ways to say *you*.
For **Sie** (polite, one or more people), take the Sie form and put the verb first: **Sie kommen** → **Kommen Sie!** For **ihr** (two or more friends or family members), take the ihr form and leave out **ihr**: **ihr kommt** → **Kommt!** For **du**, take the du form and drop **du** and the ending **-st**: **du kommst** → **Komm!** **du trinkst** → **Trink!** If the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z, only the **-t** goes: **du liest** → **Lies!** **du isst** → **Iss!** Verbs with a stem in -t or -d keep an **e**: **Arbeite!**
Verbs with the vowel change e → i or e → ie keep it in the du form: **Iss!** **Nimm!** **Sprich!** **Lies!** But a → ä disappears: **du fährst** → **Fahr!** **du schläfst** → **Schlaf!** With many verbs you may also add an **-e** (**Komme!**, **Schlafe!**), but this sounds formal or old-fashioned, and it is never possible with the e → i verbs.
**sein** is irregular: **Sei!** **Seid!** **Seien Sie!** Separable verbs send the prefix to the end, as always: **Ruf mich an!** **Steh auf!** **Kauft bitte ein!** Add **bitte** to make a request polite.
Careful: in the Sie form, **Sie** must stay: **Kommen Sie!** In the du form, leave out **du** (**Komm!**, not **Du komm!**) and drop the **-st** (**Trink!**, not **Trinkst!**). Also, **Ess!** and **Fähr!** are wrong; say **Iss!** and **Fahr!**

title.t: um acht Uhr, am Abend, im Mai
title.s: Time expressions: um, am, im, von … bis, ab

grammar.explain:
To say *when* something happens, German uses small prepositions. Each one goes with a certain kind of time expression, and they don't always match English.
**um** is for clock times: **um sieben Uhr**, **um halb acht**, **um Viertel nach drei**. To ask, say **Wann?** or **Um wie viel Uhr?**
**am** is for parts of the day and for days: **am Morgen**, **am Abend**, **am Montag**, **am Sonntag**. The days are **Montag**, **Dienstag**, **Mittwoch**, **Donnerstag**, **Freitag**, **Samstag** and **Sonntag**. One exception to remember: **in der Nacht** *at night*.
**im** is for months and seasons: **im Mai**, **im Juli**, **im Sommer**, **im Winter**.
**von … bis** gives a start and an end: **von acht bis vier Uhr**, **von Montag bis Freitag**. **ab** gives only the start: **ab neun Uhr** *from nine o'clock on*, **ab Montag** *starting Monday*.
Some time words need no preposition: **heute**, **heute Abend**, **jeden Tag**. And when a time expression starts the sentence, the verb still comes second: **Am Montag arbeite ich.**
Careful: English says *at* seven, *on* Monday, *in* the morning and *at* night, so it's easy to mix them up. German says **um sieben Uhr**, **am Montag**, **am Morgen** and **in der Nacht**, and never **in Mai** or **am Mai**. Persian often uses no preposition with clock times, but German needs **um**: **Ich komme um acht Uhr.**
